n: Absalom begins to act like a king in waiting, riding in a chariot with fifty runners ahead of him — a public display of royal status.

f.w: fifty men to run before him
f.g: Runners in front of a chariot were a sign of royalty.

n: Every morning he stations himself by the city gate, where people came to have their legal cases heard by the king. He greets each one personally, asking where they are from.

f.g: The city gate was where legal and public business took place.
A legal dispute or lawsuit.

n: He tells each person that their case is good, but the king has no one to hear it — subtly blaming his father’s government for neglect.

f.g: Appointed, assigned.

n: “If only I were judge,” he says, “I would give everyone justice.” It is the oldest political tactic: promise everything and blame the current leader.

f.g: A legal case or complaint.

n: When people bow to him, Absalom instead takes their hand and kisses them, acting like their equal and friend.

f.g: A gesture of warm familiarity rather than royal distance.

n: In this way Absalom “stole the hearts” of Israel — winning loyalty through flattery and deception rather than true service.

f.g: Deceived them; won their affection dishonestly. Compare Genesis 31:20, where “stole away unawares” is literally “stole the heart.”

n: Absalom asks to go to Hebron to fulfill a religious vow. The “forty years” is likely a copying error; some ancient versions read “four years.”

f.g: Several ancient versions read “four years,” which fits the timeline better.
Absalom’s birthplace and David’s first capital — a symbolic place to claim the throne.

n: He claims he had promised to worship the Lord in Hebron if God brought him home. He uses religion as a cover for rebellion.
David sends him off with “Go in peace” — the last words he will ever speak to his son. The irony is painful.

f.g: Hebrew lek beshalom; the name Absalom means “father of peace.”

n: Absalom secretly sends agents throughout Israel, ready to proclaim him king at a trumpet signal.

f.g: Secret messengers or agents.

n: Two hundred guests from Jerusalem go with him innocently, unaware of the plot. Their presence makes it look as if leading citizens support Absalom.

f.g: Innocently, without knowing the plan.

n: Absalom recruits Ahithophel, David’s most trusted adviser — possibly Bath-sheba’s grandfather. The rebellion grows stronger by the day.

f.g: A town in the hill country of Judah.

n: A messenger brings David the alarming news: the people’s loyalty has shifted to Absalom.
David decides to flee Jerusalem at once, partly to spare the city from a bloody siege. He chooses retreat rather than fighting in the streets.

f.w: smite the city with the edge of the sword
f.g: David wished to protect Jerusalem’s people from violence.

n: David’s servants pledge their loyalty, ready to follow wherever he leads.
David leaves with his household, leaving ten concubines to care for the palace — a detail that will matter when Nathan’s prophecy is fulfilled.
The king and his people stop at “the far house,” perhaps the last house on the edge of the city.

f.w: a place that was far off
f.g: Literally “the far house” — possibly the last house before leaving the city.

n: His loyal troops march past him in review: the royal bodyguard and six hundred soldiers from Gath who had joined him.

f.w: the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites

f.g: Men from Gath, Philistine soldiers who had become loyal to David.

n: David urges Ittai, a Philistine newcomer, to go back and serve the new king rather than share David’s uncertain fate. He is a foreigner and owes David nothing.

f.w: a stranger, and also an exile
f.g: A foreigner who had already lost his own homeland.

n: David generously releases him: why should he wander with a fugitive king? He blesses him with steadfast love and faithfulness.

f.g: Ḥesed and ’emet — loyal love and faithfulness.

n: Ittai’s reply is one of the great statements of loyalty in scripture: wherever the king goes, in life or death, he will go too. A foreigner shows more faithfulness than David’s own son.

f.w: whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be

n: David accepts, and Ittai crosses over with all his men and their families.

f.g: Children and dependents.

n: The whole countryside weeps as the king crosses the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem toward the wilderness. Centuries later, Jesus would cross the same brook on the night of His betrayal.

f.g: A valley between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives.

n: The priests Zadok and Abiathar bring the ark with the Levites, setting it down until everyone has left the city.

f.w: the ark of the covenant of God

n: David sends the ark back. He will not use it as a good-luck charm; if God favors him, God will bring him back to see it again.

f.w: Carry back the ark of God into the city

f.g: His dwelling — the tent where the ark resided.

n: And if God has rejected him, David submits humbly: “Let him do to me as seemeth good.” His trust in God’s will is a model of meek faith.

f.w: let him do to me as seemeth good unto him

n: David asks Zadok, a seer, to return to Jerusalem with the two priests’ sons, who will serve as his messengers.

f.g: One who sees by revelation; or “Do you see?” — the Hebrew is debated.

n: David will wait by the fords of the Jordan in the wilderness until word arrives from them.

f.g: Inform me with reliable news.

n: The priests carry the ark back to Jerusalem and stay there.

David climbs the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered and barefoot, with all his people weeping too. The rejected king, betrayed by those close to him, going up Olivet in sorrow, foreshadows Jesus’ own suffering there.

f.g: The Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron.

f.w: had his head covered, and he went barefoot
f.g: Signs of mourning and humiliation.

n: When David learns his wise counselor Ahithophel has joined the conspiracy, he prays immediately that God will turn Ahithophel’s advice into foolishness.

f.w: turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness

n: At the summit, where people worshipped, David’s prayer begins to be answered: his friend Hushai arrives in mourning.

f.g: The Archites were a clan living near Bethel, on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin.

f.w: his coat rent, and earth upon his head

n: David tells Hushai, probably an older man, that he would only slow them down if he came along.
Instead, Hushai can serve him better by going back to Jerusalem, pretending loyalty to Absalom, and countering Ahithophel’s advice from the inside.

f.g: Defeat = frustrate, thwart.

n: Hushai can pass anything he learns to the priests Zadok and Abiathar.
Their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan will carry messages to David — a network of loyal spies.
Hushai enters Jerusalem just as Absalom arrives. Both men reach the city at the same moment, and the contest of counsel is set to begin.

f.g: Possibly an official title, “the King’s Friend” — a trusted royal adviser (1 Chronicles 27:33).
